items.s: The firm sells the customer shares out of its own inventory and is paid a mark-up.
items.w: Trading from inventory is principal capacity, and the firm’s only fee is the mark-up or mark-down.

items.s: The firm matches a willing buyer with a willing seller and never owns the security.
items.w: In agency capacity the firm only matches two counterparties and does not purchase or own the shares.

items.s: The firm charges each of the two matched customers a commission.
items.w: Agency trades are paid by commission, and both matched clients may be charged one.

items.s: The customer sells shares to the firm and receives a price reduced by a mark-down.
items.w: A firm buying from the client as principal compensates itself through a mark-down, not a commission.

items.s: The firm’s entitlement to earn a profit is a factor in setting its charge.
items.w: The right to make a profit is a fair-pricing factor for principal trades only, per the Knopman Note.

items.s: A trade can occur only when two other participants want to transact on the same terms at the same time.
items.w: Agency requires two outside counterparties on agreeable terms at once, since the firm is not a party.

items.s: The firm holds inventory and capital ready to deploy, adding liquidity through position trading.
items.w: Position trading from inventory is how dealers provide near-instant execution and add liquidity to the market.

items.s: Each listed security has exactly one designated market maker assigned to it.
items.w: The NYSE assigns one DMM per security, whereas Nasdaq can have many market makers in one stock.

items.s: Trading occurs in an auction market combining floor trading with simultaneous electronic trading.
items.w: The NYSE uses a dual-method approach of human floor trading plus electronic trading of the same securities.

items.s: There is no central trading location, and every transaction occurs electronically.
items.w: Nasdaq is exclusively electronic with no central location and no DMM-like figure overseeing trading.

items.s: It was the world’s first electronic stock exchange.
items.w: Nasdaq earned that distinction, while the NYSE is simply the world’s largest exchange.

items.s: Market makers must post bid and ask quotations, making it a negotiated marketplace.
items.w: Nasdaq is described as negotiated because competing market makers must post two-sided quotes to trade.

items.s: It is the world’s largest stock exchange, ahead of Nasdaq.
items.w: The chapter calls the NYSE the largest exchange and Nasdaq the second largest behind it.

items.s: Human oversight is concentrated around the open, the close and volatile periods.
items.w: DMMs have special importance at the open, close and heightened volatility, which is unique to the NYSE.

items.s: Quoted issuers must have registered under the ’33 Act and keep filing 10-Ks and 10-Qs.
items.w: OTCBB issuers must be current in ’34 Act reports, which is the key contrast with OTC Pink.

items.s: Quoted companies are not required to file periodic reports or audited financials with the SEC.
items.w: OTC Pink has no ’34 disclosure requirement, making reliable information hard to find on its issuers.

items.s: It was formerly known as the Pink Sheets, named for the paper quotes were printed on.
items.w: OTC Markets, also called OTC Pink, took its name from the pink paper used for historic quotes.

items.s: It is a FINRA-operated quotation service, and FINRA planned to close it at the end of 2021.
items.w: The OTCBB was run by FINRA, and the Knopman Note says FINRA would shut it down by end of 2021.

items.s: Quotes on this venue may be one-sided, with only a bid or only an ask.
items.w: The Knopman Note says OTC Pink quotes may be one-sided, unlike the required two-sided exchange quotes.

items.s: Its quoted securities include regional and foreign equities, warrants, ADRs and direct participation programs.
items.w: The chapter lists those instrument types specifically as OTCBB securities with real-time quotes and volume.

items.s: It has no formal listing requirements, and many quoted companies are closely held or extremely small.
items.w: OTC Pink imposes no formal listing standards, so tiny, thinly traded and closely held issuers dominate it.

title: Front-running vs Trading ahead of customers

items.s: A rep learns of a client’s pending 25,000-share buy order and first buys for a personal account.
items.w: Trading on knowledge of an imminent block order before it executes is classic front-running under Rule 5270.

items.s: The firm buys 500 shares for inventory at $20 while holding an unexecuted customer buy limit at $20.
items.w: Trading for the firm’s own account at a price equal to or better than a customer limit triggers Rule 5320.

items.s: The concern involves material, nonpublic information about an imminent block trade of 10,000 shares or more.
items.w: Rule 5270 centers on nonpublic knowledge of a block, generally an order of 10,000 shares or more.

items.s: The firm cures the situation by filling the customer’s order at the same or a better price within 60 seconds.
items.w: Rule 5320 permits the firm’s trade only if the customer limit order is filled promptly for at least the same shares.

items.s: The rule does not apply if the trader was unaware of the customer’s unexecuted limit order.
items.w: Lack of awareness of the customer’s order is an express exception to the trading-ahead prohibition.

items.s: The regulatory fear is that the large customer order will push the price up after the insider’s small order.
items.w: Front-running profits when a known large order later moves the price in the insider’s favor.

items.s: Institutional clients who received written disclosure may be excluded from the protection.
items.w: Written disclosure at account opening or before each trade lets firms trade ahead of institutional clients.

items.s: It guarantees the price or better but does not guarantee that the order will execute.
items.w: A limit order protects the price, yet it never fills if the specified price is unavailable.

items.s: Once the stop price trades, it becomes a market order and may fill at a worse price than the stop.
items.w: A triggered stop is a market order, so execution can be above or below the stop price (gap risk).

items.s: It is filled at the first price that satisfies the specified price or better.
items.w: The chapter says limit orders are filled at the first price that satisfies the limit.

items.s: It can be partially filled if the full quantity is not available at the specified price.
items.w: The chapter contrasts limit orders, which may be partially filled, with stop orders that are fully executed.

items.s: A sell version protects profit on an existing long position by triggering as the price falls.
items.w: A sell stop below the market locks in gains and limits losses on a long stock position.

items.s: A buy version entered below the market is used to purchase at a cheaper price.
items.w: Buy limits sit below the market because customers want to buy cheaper than the current price.

items.s: A buy version caps potential losses on a short sale by repurchasing the shares if the price rises.
items.w: A buy stop above the market protects a short position, which otherwise has unlimited loss potential.

items.s: A buy limit at 45 entered when the stock trades at 50.
items.w: Buy limit orders are placed below the current market, so they fall in the BLiSS group.

items.s: A sell limit at 55 entered when the stock trades at 50.
items.w: Sell limits sit above the market, which makes them SLoBS orders that are not adjusted.

items.s: A sell stop entered to protect a long position, such as at 29 with the stock at 31.
items.w: Sell stops are entered below the market, so they belong with BLiSS orders.

items.s: A buy stop entered to protect a short position, such as at 110 with the stock at 105.
items.w: Buy stops are entered above the market and are classed as SLoBS orders.

items.s: On the ex-dividend date, the order’s limit or stop price is automatically reduced by the cash dividend unless DNR is attached.
items.w: Orders entered below the market are lowered by the dividend, and only a DNR instruction prevents it.

items.s: The order price is left unchanged on the ex-dividend date even without a DNR instruction.
items.w: Orders above the market are not adjusted for dividends because the price drop cannot trigger them.

items.s: A sell stop at 47.50 with the stock at 50 becomes 46.25 after a $1.25 dividend.
items.w: A sell stop is below the market, so it is cut by the dividend to avoid inadvertent triggering.
